strengths: R2E presents a coherent contribution to retrieval-based NLP: candidate-specific evidence retrieval, masked entity representations, and a compact set transformer enable quantitative attribution to passages actually used in scoring. Updating the evidence corpus without retraining is a useful capability.

The literature evaluations include meaningful safeguards: training encoders from scratch, temporal cutoffs, document-level splits, and separation of training queries from retrieved evidence. Gene-balanced metrics and the additional genetics-coverage-restricted evaluation improve experimental rigor.

The results support the stated predictive contribution. Gene Description Facts MRR improves from 0.167 for MLM to 0.260 for corrected R2E; updated retrieval improves 2022 literature MRR from 0.205 to 0.219. Literature-based clinical performance matches MLM, while genetics-only R2E improves AUROC over the genetics baseline from 0.545 to 0.579.

The appendices provide substantial architecture, optimization, attribution, prompting, ablation, and runtime details, supporting reimplementation of the core method. The reported release of three evaluation datasets is a useful community contribution, and the qualitative analyses acknowledge concrete model and auditing failures.
weaknesses: The explanation claims need a narrower interpretation. Shapley values attribute a fixed retrieved-set score relative to the learned NULL baseline; they do not establish biological correctness or reveal the model's complete reasoning. Clinical evidence relevance AUROC is only 0.665, and human validation covers eight hypotheses with one expert. Agreement between GPT-4 and that expert does not directly establish R2E–human alignment. Direct expert evaluation and attribution stability measurements would strengthen this central contribution.

The prospective clinical interpretation is only partially supported. The literature has a pre-2005 cutoff, but the genetics evidence comes from a 2024 source without a corresponding temporal restriction, and GPT-4 auditing introduces knowledge with a later cutoff. Combined and audited results therefore require separate retrospective framing. Furthermore, Appendix P labels discontinued Phase II/III programs as failures and pre-registration or later programs as successes; these are imperfect proxies for demonstrated efficacy and regulatory approval, despite the acknowledged label noise.

The comparisons do not fully isolate the architectural advantage. Appendix G describes frequency correction for MLM, but the main comparisons apply it only to R2E, leaving part of the balanced-ranking improvement insufficiently controlled. Stronger retrieval or evidence-ranking baselines would also help establish broader merits. The additional clinical gains from genetics integration and auditing are small; uncertainty estimates and sensitivity to shared targets, diseases, or drugs would strengthen their interpretation.

Exact empirical reproduction remains difficult despite the detailed method description. Training and retrieval depend on licensed literature and a proprietary entity-linking pipeline, while code and weights are explicitly withheld. Public evaluation sets alone do not reproduce these inputs. A documented configuration using public literature and an accessible linker would substantially improve independent verification.

Appendix F contains a correctable theoretical inconsistency. Negative sampling excludes the positive entity, so its conditional distribution is (1 - p(a|q))/(N - 1), rather than the query-independent 1/N assumed in Equation 9. The optimal binary logit consequently includes an additional -log(1 - p(a|q)) term. Uncorrected ranking remains monotonic in p(a|q), but the exact PMI interpretation of the subsequent correction needs qualification.
